en: The Treatise on the Object-Condition (*Ālambanaparīkṣā*),
composed by the Bodhisattva Dignāga,
translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Xuanzang by Imperial Decree.

Regarding those who wish to maintain that external forms serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses, such as visual consciousness, they either assert that atoms (*paramāṇu*) possess substantial reality because they can produce consciousness,
or they assert that it is the composite (*saṃghāta*), because when consciousness arises, it bears the aspect (*ākāra*) of that [composite].
Both [positions] are unreasonable. Why is this so?
Because, with respect to the five consciousnesses, even if atoms were conditions, they would not be objects of perception.
Because that [object] lacks the characteristic of being perceived, it is like the visual faculty and so forth.

As for the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*): it refers to that which the perceiving consciousness brings along as its aspect when arising, and which exists as a substantial entity such that the perceiving consciousness relies upon it to come into being.

If the atoms of form and so forth possessed substantial reality capable of producing the five consciousnesses, they might be considered objects in the sense of being causal conditions; however, they are not the *ālambana* (objective referents), because—just as the eye-faculty and so forth are not the objective referents for the visual consciousness and the others—they lack the specific images corresponding to those consciousnesses.
In this way, atoms have no status as objects for visual consciousness and the other sensory cognitions.
Even if they were combined, they would not be objects for the five consciousnesses;
since their substance does not truly exist, they are like a second moon.

Because the combination of form and other factors possesses that appearance within visual consciousness and the like, they may be posited as objects of cognition; however, they lack the actual status of being an object.

Just as one with impaired vision sees a second moon which lacks substantial reality and cannot produce [a valid perception], so too this combination lacks the status of being an object for visual consciousness and the others.
Therefore, regarding the two external factors, it is equally illogical for them to lack one of the two branches of the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).

Some maintain that each [atom] such as form possesses multiple characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and among these, one portion is the object of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); thus, the atoms mutually support one another, each possessing a single characteristic of aggregation (*saṃcita-lakṣaṇa*).

If it is argued that these images truly exist and each can produce a consciousness that appears similar to itself, and therefore they serve as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the five consciousnesses,
this too is irrational. Why is this so?
Just as solidity and so forth, even if they were the objects of visual consciousness and the like,
would be conditions but not objective supports (*ālambana*), because they are admitted to have the characteristics of atoms (*paramāṇu*).

Although characteristics such as solidity exist substantially, they may function as conditions for visual consciousness and the like, yet they are not objective supports, because those characteristics do not appear within visual consciousness and the like.

The principle regarding the characteristics of the aggregation of atoms of form and so forth should likewise be understood in this way, for they both maintain that these are the characteristics of atoms.
Furthermore, there is another error in maintaining that the visual consciousness and other such cognitions can take the aggregated characteristics of atoms as their objects.
Regarding the conceptual cognitions of jars, bowls, and so forth, those attachments should not differ;
for they do not differ because of differences in shape, since differences in shape are not real.

Since objects such as jars and bowls are equal in size and so on, the atoms that constitute them are equal in number; therefore, the conceptual cognitions directed toward them should likewise be without distinction.
If it is argued that the cognition differs because the forms of those objects differ, this is also logically untenable.
Distinct shapes such as "the top" exist only in conventional phenomena like jars and the like, and do not pertain to atoms.
One should not maintain that atoms also possess differentiated shapes. Why is this?
Because atoms are equal in magnitude, the distinction of shape exists only conventionally.
When those [objects] are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*), the cognition of them is necessarily abandoned.

Since jars, bowls, and the like cannot constitute ultimate atoms, and since the distinct dimensions and shapes abandon the spherical characteristic (*parimaṇḍala*) of the atom, we know that distinct shapes exist only conventionally and are not real.
Furthermore, when distinct shapes are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms, the cognition of them is necessarily abandoned;
however, the cognition of substances such as blue does not cease when they are analyzed down to their ultimate atoms.

Therefore, distinct shapes exist only conventionally and do not reside in real entities like blue and other colors do. Consequently, it is thoroughly established that the nature of the objective condition for the five consciousnesses is not external form and so forth.
Is it the case that its object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) does not exist at all?
It is not entirely non-existent. If so, how is it?

Internal form appears as if external; it is accepted as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for consciousness because its aspect resides within consciousness and because it can produce consciousness.
Although external objects do not exist, internal form appears resembling an external object and serves as the objective condition.
It is granted that the visual and other consciousnesses arise bearing the images of those [objects] and are produced from them, because they possess these two characteristics.
Since this internal objective image is not separate from consciousness, how can it act as a condition for consciousness when they arise simultaneously?
Because they are determined to follow one another, they act as conditions for each other simultaneously;
or rather, the preceding acts as a condition for the succeeding, because it draws forth its functional capacity.
Since the objective aspect (*viṣaya-ākāra*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are necessarily concomitant, even though they arise at the same time, the former serves as a condition for the latter.
The proponents of *hetuvidyā* (logic) say:
If this and that follow one another in terms of presence and absence, then even though they arise simultaneously, they may still possess the relationship of cause and effect.

Alternatively, the aspect of a preceding consciousness serves as the condition for a subsequent consciousness, inducing the arising of a capacity within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*) that produces a semblance of its own result; this does not contradict reason.
If the five consciousnesses arise by taking only internal form as their object, how can it also be said that the eye and so forth are their conditions?
The capacity for cognition within form is appropriately termed the "five faculties";
this capacity and its objective form have served as mutual causes since beginningless time.

Because consciousness can arise, one infers the existence of the sense faculties (indriya). These are merely functional capacities (śakti) and are not produced by external matter; therefore, it is not contrary to reason to designate the fivefold functional capacities upon the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) as the "eye-faculty" and so forth, since there is no difference in principle regarding these capacities giving rise to consciousness.

Although it cannot be said that [the object] exists either in consciousness or elsewhere, since external phenomena do not exist in principle, one must necessarily admit that this [object] exists in consciousness and nowhere else.
The functional capacity of these faculties and the objective forms of the preceding moments have served as reciprocal causes from beginningless time.

That is to say, when this functional capacity reaches its state of maturation, it produces the five internal objective forms upon the manifest consciousness; these internal objective forms, in turn, are able to induce the functional capacities of the five sense organs upon the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).
Are the two types of form—the sense faculty and the object—and consciousness identical or different? Or are they neither identical nor different?

One may explain this according to one's preference; thus it is well established by reason that these various consciousnesses take only the internal objective aspect as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
